People regularly talk about owning real estate or buying private land, but in reality they don't really own it.

Apart from the obvious, that they are still subjects of whatever government's borders they happen to fall within and subject to their laws, in practice their "ownership" of the land is really more like a lease from the government. The lease might not have an official expiry date, and you might not have bought it directly from the government (more likely another leaseholder) but nonetheless, you're required to pay rent (property tax) and at any time the government can cancel the lease and serve a compulsory purchase order, with or without compensation.

In any state which recognises eminent domain, there is only one private land owner: The law.

That's a great question. In the US the government claims ownership of wilderness land, and the "right" of eminent domain over everything else - which as you say practically amounts to a claim of ownership.

In England (and I think all/most of Europe) since at least 1066 the prevailing legal theory has been that all land is owned by the state; anyone else only ever being granted possession conditionally and revocably.

In japan they had an even more complex system: The emperor owned all the land, the peasants owned the produce of the land, and the samurai were entitled to a portion of that produce. In theory this would put the emperor on top and the samurai at the bottom, in practice it made the samurai the most powerful and the emperor dependent on their benevolence. Several emperors were forced to pass legislation by the simple expedient of cutting off their food supply.
